articleTitle: Power supply for the Atlantic TGV high speed line
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author discusses the 2*25 kV AT (autotransformer) system chosen for the Atlantic TGV lines. The system has two essential advantages: control of the current return circuit and less induced interference on weak current lines; and fewer voltage drops on the line because power is transmitted under 50 kV between the substation and autotransformers; impedance in the power feed circuit is lower therefore and substations are spaced two to two and a half times farther apart than with 25 kV single-phase AC for equal performance levels. The author discusses the HV power supply for single-phase substations, substation design and implementation, OCS feeder line power feed, and features of the electrical equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Public supply disturbance from AC traction
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Electricity supply authorities are increasingly expected to supply disturbing loads, i.e. to railways who do not take a balanced 3-phase current and/or a sinusoidal current waveform. Consequently the supply voltages acquire these irregularities and could make other customers' equipment maloperate. The causes and effects are briefly explained. An AC traction supply is a type of disturbing load in two respects. It inherently requires a single phase supply and the locomotive takes a rectangular current waveform. The author gives guidance on predicting the likely disturbances based on years of experience in the UK. An illustration is given of the calculation. The emphasis is on the prediction of disturbances. For brevity it is assumed that traction supplies are via 132/25 kV single phase transformers, connected line to line.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of static shunt compensation to upgrade existing electrified railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: When 25 kV AC railway power supplies are designed, the electrical capacity is arranged to suit future levels of traffic, which are predicted to occur several years after the start of electrified operation. As traffic levels grow, the spare capacity is gradually used up until the load reaches the design limit. Beyond this point operating difficulties can occur, the two main problems being excessive catenary current and low catenary voltage. On a number of railway systems, the design capacity has been reached and various means of increasing the traffic capacity have been investigated. As a consequence, several railway authorities in different parts of the world are considering methods of improving their electrical capacity. Several means of upgrading the power supply system are possible, each with particular advantages and disadvantages. Some of these are considered by the authors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A concept for an HVDC traction system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: It is a well-known fact that single phase AC is not the most ideal railway electrification system. A DC system has obviously many advantages to the single-phase AC system. However, so far the limited system voltage has been a considerable drawback. The authors present a quite realistic system, which permits high system voltages. To some extent the ideas are not new, but the application is interesting and makes HVDC electrifications a possibility today. The concept of the proposed HVDC traction system is based on a conventional HVDC transmission system, a technology which is well established today.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Single-phase 25kV electrification of Sardinia railway: some particular problems related to an electrified railway located in an island
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Italian railways are in the process of electrifying the main railway trunk of the Sardinia island because of future railway traffic increases which will probably make the use of diesel locomotives disadvantageous in a few years. The so called 'Dorsale Sarda' will connect the most important cities of the island from Cagliari to Sassari and Olbia passing through Oristano. The authors examine the technical reasons behind the use of a 25 kV, 50 Hz system and describe the benefits of such a system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PWM converter-inverter system for AC supplied train
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Japan Railways are applying an AC drive system to AC supplied trains. They first convert AC industrial frequency into DC with a PWM converter, and then convert DC in to 3-phase variable voltage variable frequency AC with PWM inverter. The authors propose new control methods of the converter-inverter system to suppress current beat of the induction motor and magnetic bias of the main transformer. And both of them have been confirmed by using computer simulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Whole system simulator for AC railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: A computer-based multi-train AC simulator is developed. This general software package, written in Fortran 77, can be used for studying power consumption and train performance in single phase AC supplied railways. The simulator is constructed with full consideration of accuracy of traction equipment modelling and flexibility and efficiency of multi-train simulation. The developed simulator is used to study a proposal for a suburban railway application with a single power feeding source, applied to a 30 km section of double track. With 12 trains operating on this system, with a one second update, the simulation time for a eight minute headway operation was less than 7.5 minutes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evolution of the electrical equipment of TGV trainsets
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Although only eight years separate the respective service introductions of the TGV Atlantique and its predecessor the TGV Paris-South-East, the main feature of this second generation of high speed rolling stock is a significant evolution of the electrical part. Due to the continuing technological developments within electronics and microcomputer fields, every electrical and electronic system was affected. The author discusses the traction line, and the computer system for control and command of all train-borne equipment. The traction system chosen was synchronous motors supplied by current convertors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modern control and power electronics for the AC drives of the German high-speed train ICE
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: On May 1, 1988, when the ICE/V high-speed experimental train of the German Federal Railways (DB) reached the world record speed of 406.9 km/h, it was the first time that the public at large was presented with the future train in high-speed rail traffic. The electric traction equipment of such a forward looking means of traffic must logically represent the latest state of the art. Two development trends in particular characterize the technology. The first is the use of microprocessors for the complete control of the traction system and the second is the use of GTO thyristors for the converters. Siemens innovated the drive system taken from the class BR 120 locomotive of DB for the ICE/V by the development of a microcomputer traction control and a GTO converter. The microcomputer traction control is used for all 82 series power cars, the GTO converters will be provided for the second half of the series power cars.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Harmonic problems in Queensland Railways electric traction system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Harmonic current distortion due to thyristor controlled locomotives is a well known fact to most railway engineers. The significance of such distortion, however, is dependent entirely on the proportion of the harmonic load to the power capacity of the electricity supply system. The author discusses the experience of Queensland Railways with respect to harmonics. Real time measurements were performed and load variations recorded. Simulation studies were also made to assist in predicting future load and consequently the harmonic level. To overcome the excessive harmonic levels it was decided that filters should be installed at all feeder stations in order to meet the standard requirements. The author discusses the filter design in particular the problems of capacitor failure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Whole system compatibility measurements of the autotransformer supplied 50 kV railway in New Zealand
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: New Zealand Railway Corporation (NZRC) have completed the electrification of the central section of the North Island Main Trunk (NIMT) and electrified commercial operation began in 1988. Because of the many novel features of this railway electrification, Hawker Siddeley Rail Projects (HSRP) were required to undertake a detailed compatibility study of all electrical sub-systems by NZRC, at the design stage. During the design process, new computer based methods of analysing the effects of loco operation on low power signalling and telecommunication circuits, as well as on the Electrocorp power system, were developed at the University of Birmingham. The simulator developed was used to confirm design choices relating to telecommunication cable earthing, the degree of electromagnetic screening which could be realistically achieved and the likely values of rail to earth voltages in the nominally earth insulated traction supply system. The authors discuss the EMC requirements and the test programme. The results for signalling, a locomotive, a substation and the telecommunication cables are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimization design on series tuning filtering and reactive compensation used in traction systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: According to the characteristics of harmonics generated by railway traction systems and the practical requirements for filtering in the system, some useful and important concepts (factors or ratios) are defined, such as filterability, reactive power distribution factor, reactive and negative sequence ratios, etc. Therefore, an optimization design method and corresponding algorithms are developed for multiarm single-tuning filtering and comprehensive compensation. These concepts are directly used in optimization design so the method is convenient and effective. As a preliminary application, comprehensive compensation performance in two feeding patterns is analysed and compared.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition monitoring of pantographs
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In order to intercept faulty pantographs before catastrophic damage is caused a method has been developed of monitoring the condition of pantographs by measuring the behaviour of the OHLE as a pantograph passes. A prototype system has been installed at a site on the West Coast Main Line (WCML) about 56 km from Euston Station on a section of line where there are up to 120 train passes per day at speeds up to 176 km/h and where the track is on an embankment exposed to the prevailing Westerly winds. Hence a high proportion of the electric locomotive fleet of the WCML can be monitored at frequent intervals, and in addition information can be obtained on the behaviour of pantographs in the varying environmental conditions in which they are required to operate.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power factor correction in a 25 KV electrified railway
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Kowloon-Canton Railway (KCR) is a 34 km double-tracked and electrified railway carrying an average of 450000 passengers a day at 1989 level. After commissioning of the system in 1982, the power factor at the supply point, as measured by the ratio of integrated half-hour MW to integrated half hour MVA, was consistently and substantially below 0.85 which was the minimum value demanded by the power supply company. The authors show typical power factor and demand profiles, and present methods for the correction of such power factors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fault diagnosis on modern three-phase traction vehicles
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Traction vehicles with high power and for high speeds are increasingly being supplied with three-phase drive systems, the majority of them are of the asynchronous type, in which the asynchronous motors are fed at variable frequency by self-commutated static converters. Control of the drives as well as the higher-order functions for the vehicle and, possibly, the train too, is performed by highly integrated microcomputer systems. Automated vehicles with variable-speed drives are very complex systems. Faults, especially in the region of the converter and process control, do not make themselves apparent by steadily increasing wear, and therefore cannot be predicted. Hence, on such vehicles the rapid determination of the cause of a fault is eminently important. The authors show how, in such cases, diagnostic facilities can render valuable help.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Continuous automatic train control and cab signalling with the LZB 80
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Austrian Federal Railway (OBB) was the first authority outside of Germany to employ the LZB 80 signalling system for high-performance locomotives and the L72 vehicle control centres. Trial operations on the new Vienna-Salzburg high-speed railway line are to begin in 1991. The entire system of continuous automatic train control comprises line and vehicle equipment for the exchange of signals via track conductor loops. Here, the author deals with just the vehicle equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The overhead system of the TGV-Atlantique
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors briefly describe two accidents on the South-East TGV line, their common cause, and subsequent solutions to prevent further similar accidents. The experience gained was incorporated into the design of the overhead line of the TGV Atlantique. The authors discuss geometry of the overhead conductors and pantographs, and the civil engineering aspects of the new line.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Supply system characteristics and harmonic penetration studies of the new high speed FS railway line 'Milan-Rome-Naples'
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Milan-Rome-Naples, main railway connection of the Italian State Railways (FS) network, is characterized by very intense traffic, with the existing lines already having reached their saturation limit. New lines are to be constructed to increase the passenger and goods transport on this connection and to improve the quality of the service. The sizing of the fixed electric traction installation has been devised in such a way that high power can be collected from the contact wire; the traction load for the design project has been assumed as trains travelling 15 minutes apart and maximum unit power demand equal to 12 MW. The authors discuss the possibilities of increasing the voltage to 12 kV DC and the problems this would create for the catenary system, power supply and power conversion system. The electric substations, harmonic penetration studies and catenary system are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Economic justification of the TGV and development of the high-speed rail system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: With the current success of the TGV Southeast and the imminent commissioning of the TGV Atlantique, the TGV projects to be completed in France in the mid-90's, will make up a real high-speed rail system. Here, the author describes the various construction phases of this system and reviews the methods used for the economic appraisal of the TGV projects. The other projects under consideration are also introduced.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microprocessor based protection for AC railway supplies
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Apart from being for single phase supplies, the protective relay requirements of AC traction substations are very similar to those of power systems in general. The authors look at the distance protection of AC track feeders and present the design of a new distance relay for AC traction feeder protection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital simulation for solution of oscillatory overvoltage problems in AC railroad electrification
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The University of Birmingham, UK, and the University of Pisa, Italy worked together to look at continuous over-voltages in the AC Dorsale Sarda railway system. Different simulation approaches are applied to the same study, the first based on a complex general purpose program and the second on a simpler program developed for such an application. Good agreement on simulation results encourages a comparison between the two methods taking into account difficulty in modelling approach, output capabilities, need of computer memory and computation times.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Supply of electricity for electrified lines in Finland
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The decision to electrify the railways in Finland was taken in 1965. The author shows how the use of power electronics on tractive stock made it possible to choose the 25 kV 50 Hz electrification system. As a result, the feeding system could be made as simple as possible. Energy is fed to electrified lines by means of single-phase transformers connected directly between two phases of the national grid. Thus the railways need no power stations or energy transmission lines of their own.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The significance and technical-economic benefits of developing railway electrification in China
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: According to China's conditions, the railway network is a main-stay backbone in all kinds of traffic systems. Statistics suggest that passenger and freight turnover fulfilled by railways in 1987 accounted for 56.1% and 71.8% respectively of the total turnover (not including oceangoing transportation) of traffic systems. By the end of 1987, the mainland state-owned railway system was operating a route kilometerage amounting to 52600 km, which is about 30600 km more than that in 1949. Confronted with these conditions, through 20 years of exploration and operating practice and taking into account the energy resource structure in China, railway electrification has been affirmed as the main effective way to reform Chinese railway transportation and to accomplish its modernization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of high power GTO inverter drives for low signalling interference currents
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In industrial AC drives the main emphasis is on minimising the total harmonic distortion due to the harmonic currents in the motor so as to achieve an improved motor performance. It is the relatively unsophisticated power frequency (33-125 Hz) and the reed relay type of track circuits (typically 360-425 Hz) which cause the most concern. Apart from the higher amplitude of the low frequency harmonics generated by the equipment and the lower attenuation of the inverter input filter, these track circuits are usually not securely coded and therefore, pass band invasion represents a potential hazard rather than a 'fail-safe' situation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of multivoltage locos for international service
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The vehicles which are described consist of two locomotives and eighteen coaches and are designed to run London-Paris and London-Brussels through the Channel Tunnel. To minimise the journey time from city centre to city centre a cruising speed of 300 kph on 25 kV lines will be used in France and Belgium. Track and power supply restrictions will initially restrict UK speeds to 160 kph. To achieve the power required for 300 kph within the allowed weight limit of 68 tonnes requires the use of three phase asynchronous motors. The authors set out some of the constraints which have had to be considered in the design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: East Coast Main Line electrification-25 kV AC system design
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author discusses the electrification of the East Coast Main Line (ECML) using 25 kV AC systems. The traction supply points usually consist of two 132/25 kV single phase transformers fed from separate 132 kV circuits. Each transformer feeds an incoming 25 kV vacuum circuit breakers in the BR feeder station. The design of the scheme and the final outcome are looked at.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic measurement of the position of the overhead contact wire
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: For optimum electric traction current collection from overhead electrified lines, the contact wire must be correctly aligned with respect to the track. There is therefore a need for an instrument to give a rapid and accurate reading of the wire position, preferably automatically without contact, both in daylight and in darkness and in all weather conditions. The device should preferably be capable of operating from a moving vehicle (maintenance trolley or service train for example) as well a operating as a portable device for use statically. The accuracy required is about +or-10 mm in both height and stagger. The authors describe the first phase of the development of such a device.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A study of power factor correction techniques for high power AC locomotives
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors describe a comparison of power factor correction (PFC) methods, which is intended to provide guidelines for selecting equipment. In order to carry out this study, a systematic personal computer based method of power electronic circuit analysis is developed, tailored to the task of comparing traction drive systems, which the authors describe. Using this generalised simulation package a brief comparison of various power factor correction schemes is also presented, thus enabling an initial engineering assessment of the various options.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A microprocessor system for traction control
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In the mid 1970's, work on the development of an harmonic elimination pulse width modulation system (PWM) for a traction inverter was being hampered by the complexity of the digital electronics required for its implementation. The authors show how it was decided to investigate the use of one of the new eight bit microprocessors then becoming available in order to reduce this complexity. Somewhat arbitrarily, the Motorola 6800 was selected. Because of known problems with electrical noise on traction vehicles, dedicated hardware was designed, drawing on experience gained with relatively fast digital logic employed on the multiplexing system developed for the British Rail Edinburgh-Glasgow push-pull trains. The resultant PWM controller eventually formed part of the Brush contribution to the People Mover Group's Birmingham Airport Maglev vehicle.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Basic criteria for a new third generation integrated maintenance system (for transportation applications)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors present a new maintenance management system which is being studied for utilisation in transportation systems. It works according to the newest maintenance strategies (RCM (reliability centered maintenance), LCC) and it is provided with a diffuse DSS which allows both the management to intervene in the best possible way to modify the strategic plan and allows responsible employees (on various decisional levels) to properly arrange a tactical plan of intervention. Moreover, the system is provided with completely new specific algorithms for the management of particular functions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The contribution of compute simulation methods to traction propulsion development
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: A guide is given to how computer simulation may be employed in the railway traction environment. The methodology of successful simulation has been divided into three principal areas; system identification, control algorithms and modelling verification. Emphasis is placed on the need for accurate modelling, on which the design of complex drives can be reliably based. The use of good simulation is a prerequisite to advanced drive design and manufacture, giving the practising engineer insight into performance and access to results, which otherwise could not be available until a prototype was tested, if at all. Conversely, poor simulation leads to false assumptions and errors, which may leave the engineer less able to achieve design requirements than without simulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Reasonable measures for reducing harmonic disturbance in power systems caused by traction loads
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Railway electrification, especially with heavy traffic, has led to problems of adverse disturbances in power supply systems. Its focal point, at present, is harmonic distortion. The authors describe measures which can be adopted to reduce the effects of harmonics. The basic method is to fit filters in electric locomotives, which should be designed with locomotive parameters in mind.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power supply options for the proposed Sydney-Melbourne 'Very Fast Train' project
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The proposal to establish a high speed train service between Sydney and Melbourne, which became known as the 'Very Fast Train' (VFT), envisaged a dedicated rail system that would bring the two cities within three hours journey time, on an almost entirely new route of some 850 km with train speeds up to 350 km/h. The authors describe the work done to establish the options for and estimated costs of providing power for the proposal, now widely known as the VFT Project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Class 30 locomotives of New Zealand Railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: New Zealand Railways Corporation operates a predominantly freight service between Wellington and Auckland over what is known as the North Island Main Trunk (NIMT). Electrification of the central portion of the NIMT has been considered on a number of occasions to improve line capacity. In 1981 the New Zealand Government gave approval to electrify 411 km of the NIMT between Palmerston North and Hamilton. A 25 kV AC overhead supply system was chosen and 22 Class 30, 3 MW, Bo-Bo-Bo locomotives were purchased. The authors describe the equipment layout, performance, electrical equipment, and traction control strategy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Propulsion and friction braking diagnostics and self test capabilities
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Todays powerful microprocessors enable extensive diagnostic and self-test capabilities to be built into control systems on rail vehicles. This allows problems to be identified and corrected faster than in the past. The author discusses the diagnostic and self-test capabilities of the DC chopper propulsion control systems and the hydraulic friction braking control system supplied by AEG Westinghouse Transportation Systems Inc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electric traction for intercity trains
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: With the decision in 1955 to adopt 25 kV 50 Hz as the supply voltage for overhead electrification on British Railways came the requirement for locomotives to pull passenger and freight trains. The first 100 locomotives introduced in 1960 were originally numbered in the E 3000 range and later became Classes 81 and 85. These were followed by a batch of 100 Class 86 locomotives which were introduced in 1965 and 36 Class 87 locomotives which entered service in 1973. Next came the 3 APT prototype trains which saw very limited service between 1980 and 1984 and in 1987 and 1988 came the first deliveries of Class 89, 90 and Class 91 locomotives. Channel Tunnel trains using 3-phase traction motors are being specified for through services between London, Paris and Brussels. The author discusses each of these different forms of traction.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A modular design of asynchronous traction drive
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: It has been generally acknowledged that microprocessor and gate turn off thyristor (GTO) technology has made a major contribution to the advancement of variable voltage variable frequency (VVVF) inverter drives. Particular benefits include supply harmonic control and the avoidance of chopper stabilisation for DC supply systems. The authors describe one approach to the design of such a system which was intended to be applicable to locomotives, electric multiple units, and even light rail vehicles. The design is structured so that any required system can be constructed from a standard set of parts. These are then assembled into a single unit as required for the application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: GTO-the 'Turbo' in electric traction?
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In connection with the GTO the word 'turbo' has to be understood in the context of increased power and increased performance. GTO thyristors have significantly improved the performance of thyristor inverters, reduced the number of elements, weight and volume, and increased reliability and availability, enabling the general break-through of the three-phase technology in electric railway traction. The author describes the main features of the GTO thyristor, including switch-on and turn-off, and their application to traction converters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The electronic equipment of the group E402 locomotive for the Italian State Railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Power electronics and the use of asynchronous motors have made it possible to produce the locomotive within a maximum weight of 82 tons, with two-axle bogies which are much lighter than with commutator motors, and with considerably reduced unsuspended masses. The E402 locomotive has considerably more specific power than the previous Italian State Railways locomotives, despite the redundancy of various pieces of equipment on board. The authors look at its most important characteristics with particular reference to the propulsion equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A rigid beam as an alternative to the conventional caternary
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The regulations concerning electrical installations on railways stipulate a minimum contact wire height of 4.8 m. This clearance is to be maintained at the highest temperature, at the highest track position and taking into due account of contact wire oscillations. The authors look at the use of a rigid beam instead of a wire for the overhead line. Only the track bed tolerances, the effect of peaks and throughs, the mounting tolerances of the rail and the wear and tear of the collector.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Aspects of the design, construction and testing of BRB's Class 90 and 91 locomotive transformers
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The geographical differences between Britain's two main north/south rail routes are such that two locomotive specifications were justified. One designated the Class 90 with a design speed limit of 175 kph, would reinforce the west coast main line services. The other designated the Class 91 'Electra' with a design speed limit of 225 kph, would mainly serve the east coast route. The performance of the two new locomotives required differing configurations of equipment layout in general and of the main transformer in particular. Hence, two locomotive transformers for BR were in design and manufacture simultaneously. The transformers have features in common. The arrangement of the main traction secondaries, the arrangement of the tertiary windings for auxiliary supplies, the electrical insulation levels, the use of Class A insulation materials, the temperature rise limits, cooling method, and the integral construction of the main transformer with its conservator and cooling system. The transformers also have features that differ. The author discusses the design, construction and testing of the two types of transformers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mk IV passenger vehicles for East Coast Main Line electrification
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Class 91 locomotives and Mk IV train sets have been designed for daytime use on services operating at up to 225 km/h. The composition of the train sets was determined by an economic need to make maximum use of the Class 91 locomotives. The Mk IV vehicles are day coaches, the locomotives will also be used at night hauling sleeping car and mail trains at speeds of up to 160 km/h. Improvements were also required in all areas of equipment and the authors set out to cover the design approach adopted to provide a new generation of passenger vehicles.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 3 kV DC catenary upgrade to 200 km/h for Spanish Railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors highlight the main course of events leading up to the uprating of the Spanish State Railways (RENFE) 3 kV DC lines to run at 200 km/h. Three test sections of the railway are identified to test different contractors' solutions. The authors concentrate on the Balfour Beatty/Nemel solution, which has been installed in the Test Section Number 2, Villar de Chinchilla to Almansa Station. The steps taken to achieve an optimised design are demonstrated. The design process started with the existing equipment format and showed how, by using the most up to date computer techniques, it was possible to establish the overall sensitivity of key aspects of the design. These aspects, wherever practicable, are developed to fit into the existing equipment with a minimum of change.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New trend in technology of air conditioners in Japan
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In Japan, about 43000 passenger railcars are in operation and currently about 30000 cars (70%) have been provided with air conditioning equipment. Mitsubishi Electric Corporation has been engaged in the manufacture of railcar air conditioning equipment since 1950, totalling about 71000 units for about 20000 cars. They are available in a wide spectrum of types-roof mount, under floor, floor mount, and split. Reflecting the rapid progress in electronic and precision processing technologies, new developments have been made in regard to energy saving, improved comfort and reduced weight. The authors report on these new developments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power remote control-East Coast Main Line
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The electrification of the East Coast Main Line (ECML) covers some 630 track kilometres between Hitchin and Edinburgh and includes the branch from Doncaster to Leeds. The ECML Hornsey SCADA system was installed in 1986 and it controls and monitors a total of 16 outstations including a test outstation based at Hornsey Electrical Control Room. The ECML Cathcart SCADA system is the very latest of British Rail's computer/VDU based SCADA systems. These and other SCADA systems are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High performance pantograph for high speed EMUs
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In EMUs that run at the speed of over 300 km/h, there exist a number of problems to be solved for the current collecting equipment. The reduction of the rate of pantograph bounce from the catenary is the fundamental problem for the contact current collection by catenary and pantograph. Pantographs for high speed EMUs should have favourable mechanical follow up characteristics in the case of not receiving aerodynamic force and also should have suitable aerodynamic characteristics. A pantograph is developed, in accordance with the existing overhead wire structure, by studying both mechanical follow up and aerodynamic characteristics to aim at the high speed performance of over 300 km/h.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Long distance data transmission of safety information for the solid state interlocking
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: British Rail's Solid State Interlocking (SSI) uses a nonstandard baseband transmission technique for communicating with its trackside equipment. Screened twisted pair cable is used as the transmission medium for a data highway which can be accessed simply by a large number of trackside interface units distributed along the railway. The authors describes the SSI long distance terminal (LDT), as the standards converter is now called. The methods used to perform standards conversion and maintain safe operation under fault conditions are described and the application of the equipment to both point-to-point and drop-and-insert transmission systems is discussed. Test results are presented as evidence of the high level of availability expected.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: East Coast Main Line: electrification fixed equipment maintenance
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The East Coast Main Line is the most recent and significant addition to the British Rail electrified network and has interconnections into other electrified lines along its route between London King's Cross and Edinburgh. The line is in the process of being electrified, the completed part of the route being London to York and the Leeds branch. The electrification system is standard BR 25 kV single phase overhead. Incoming supplies are taken from the national grid network at 16 locations. The author looks at maintenance of the power supply, the overhead equipment, safety and performance management of the electrification equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Energy-efficient driving patterns in electric railway traction
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In recent years due to the introduction of power electronics in traction systems and auxiliary equipment, a 'loss free' voltage control has been obtained. Nevertheless Netherlands Railways Ltd. (NS) is faced with a quite significant increase of the specific traction energy consumption. Here, the authors show that in general, short running times can only be obtained at relatively high power losses. In this paper the possibilities for a consistent reduction of energy consumption are outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optical fibre telecommunication with fail safe transmission for railway utility
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Today's general demands to railway administrations all over the world are: improved traffic regularity, more frequent departures and shorter travelling times. In order to meet above demands it is paramount to expand the existing transmission capacity for telecommunication and to implement more flexible signal interlocking systems. The authors describe the advantages gained by railway administration from applying optical fibre telecommunication together with failsafe transmission for line block systems. Futhermore, the authors present projects in Denmark and India using the new technologies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Monitoring and interlocking of train operation by modern electronic equipment
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: A single, fully integrated computer system developed by AEG Westinghouse handles all functions associated with the safe operation of a mass transit system. Such functions include operator interface, mode control, vehicle tracking, vehicle routing, data acquisition, data display and vital interlocking. The system uses a distributed architecture of advanced microprocessors with the latest peripherals and display technologies. The general approach is based on the use of generic hardware with all the functions handled in the software. The author concentrates on the operator interface in the central control room and the implementation of the safety interlocking logic using microprocessors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Static power supply for DC 1500V transit system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Chopper or PWM inverter controlled electric cars have evolved out of a long history of electric railways. However, silicon rectifiers and high speed circuit breakers have been dominant in the common DC substations. The authors summarize the modern DC substation equipment delivered to the Transportation Bureau of Sapporo City Japan. Then, the revenue operation field data analyses and the short-circuit fault test results are presented. Emphases are on the GTO circuit breaker and the digital Delta I relay aspects, where Delta I gives current variation profile on a given feeder.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TVM 400-a modular and flexible ATC system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: TVM 400 is a range of ATC systems built around the same basic architecture with a consistent set of hardware and software modules. System modularity ensures compatibility: the same rolling stock can be used under different operating conditions and with different signalling equipment. The flexibility of the system permits functional (safety and speed increase, etc.) and technical (new transmission channels) improvements. TVM 400 is an open system that can fulfil from the simplest to the most sophisticated needs in train operation requirements, from speed monitoring with or without wayside signalling to fully automated operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multiplex push pull control of traction on British Rail
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: British Rail has recently initiated the industrial development of specified multiplex push pull control equipment for electric locomotive applications. The authors show how investigations were carried out in order to: assess the validity of the performance requirements in this specification; to prove the feasibility of operating processor-based equipment in the hostile environment of an electric locomotive; and to acquaint the manufacturers of the equipment with the railway environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrification of British Railways' East Coast Main Line: the project and its management
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The East Coast Main Line extends 393 miles from London to Edinburgh with a 30 mile branch from Doncaster to Leeds, and a project to electrify the route was approved by Government on 27th July, 1984. The author using simple but powerful techniques, it is possible to plan the implementation of a major railway electrification project such that it can be executed with virtually no impact on the existing service, customers or revenues. It is also possible to prepare accurate estimates of outlays such that the authorised monies are just sufficient for the task.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: After ECML-system design for main line electrification on BR
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author sets out the basic assumptions being used to examine the main options for the system design aspects of electrification fixed equipment and connections to the electricity supply industry (ESI) high voltage grid system. The first consideration is how to translate business aspirations into the required electrical terms i.e. the anticipated short-term peak and average values of the traction load. These assumptions are then used to consider railway electrification fixed equipment ratings and identify areas where new designs will have to be developed. The effect of these railway loadings on the ESI is considered against the standards for 3-phase system disturbances and anticipated development of the high voltage grid system. Last, but not least, some safety implications of higher electrical loadings are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software systems: design for maintenance railway applications
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: From the earliest days of computing, railways have made use of management information systems based on software. With the recent rapid growth of microprocessor applications, however, software has spread into areas previously untouched. Remote control systems and signalling applications such as track circuits and interlockings have all become microprocessor based. Even locomotives now contain software. This trend means that it is becoming increasingly important for railways to be able to control the development and application of software including the incorporation of changes. Here, the authors present a brief review of a number of emerging techniques which promise to make the task of software maintenance easier, and more productive.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New Zealand Railways: an overview of the North Island Main Trunk electrification
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The 410 km electrified section of the North Island Main Trunk traverses the rugged central region of the North Island of New Zealand (NZ). The author reviews the transport environment leading to the decision to electrify the route, the studies undertaken, the system and its implementation, and the economic considerations together justifying the project investment. Operating and route improvements undertaken concurrently to enhance the benefits of electrification are also discussed. The author concludes by discussing recent changes to the NZ transport scene which have affected the economic viability of the project and the commercial role of electrification for the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Feasibility study for maximum demand control on the central division of Queensland Railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Queensland Railway (QR) has electrified its Central Queensland Track servicing the mines west of Rockhampton and Mackay. The traffic task annually consumes 202*10/sup 6/ kWh of electrical energy for the Goonyella system and 161*10/sup 6/ kWh for the Blackwater system resulting in an annual electricity cost of A$29M. The existing tariff structures provided two usable tariffs; a time of use energy consumption tariff and a time of use two-part demand tariff. Considering the level of consumption and maximum demand, it became obvious to QR that minimising the upper limit of the maximum half-hour demand for the total system could save substantial annual electricity costs. This is by virtue of maintaining the load factor as high as possible and making best use of the two-part demand tariff. The authors discuss strategies to reduce and control the maximum half-hour demands.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High speed signalling in France
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Two important factors guided SNCF in its choice of high-speed line driving and signalling techniques: the higher the speed, the more difficult it is for drivers to perceive lineside signals properly; and, despite rail's excellent safety record, human beings are more failure-prone than automatic devices. As a result of these two factors, the following principles were adopted in research into driving and signalling systems: the signalling system was to be designed so that the safety of very high speed trains would not be dependent on correct observation of lineside signals; and trains were to continue to be manually operated with drivers controlling acceleration, deceleration, coasting and braking but a speed monitoring system was to be mounted to check vehicle movement in relation to the signals displayed and intervene if necessary through sharp brake application. The author discusses these principles as applied to the South East and Northern TGV lines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The informative system of high speed train ETR-500 for the Italian State Railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Italian high-speed system is expected to serve two main lines: Milan-Bologna-Florence-Rome-Naples-Battipaglia; and Turin-Venice. The trains to be assigned are ETR-500 with speed of 300 km/h and made-up of 2 electric locomotives and 10-18 cars. The author describes three systems which represent different aspects of a single on-board communication system that is quite powerful, flexible and expandable to the most sophisticated functions. In the future there will be the possibility of integrating the three systems into a single optical fiber line with a radio link for communication among vehicles. The overall system is capable of offering the most comfortable conditions for the passengers; a pressurized and air-conditioned atmosphere, HiFi and video programs, information display, telephone, telex, telefax, and communication with on-board personnel in case of emergency.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interference-free track vacancy detection
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Shortly after the opening of the first railway lines, at the beginning of the last century, it became clear that 'rules of the line' needed to be laid down if passengers were to be transported safely and operational procedures conducted smartly. As human error could never be ruled out, safely equipment had to be developed. Here, the author shows that the purpose of track vacancy detection equipment is to determine the occupancy of sections by rail vehicles. Thereby, the interlocking is supplied with vital information. He argues that automatic track vacancy detection equipment is a prerequisition for automatic train control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Channel Tunnel Shuttle locomotives, an overview of the design process
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors discuss the factors affecting design and selection of the locomotives for the Channel Tunnel. The main factors considered are the tunnel infrastructure and the operating performance requirements. The authors concentrate on the installed power, mechanical parts and reliability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The influence of rotating machine design standards on the design of traction supplies
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Railway traction loads, because they are single-phase, produce unbalanced currents which in turn cause unbalanced voltages in the supply system. Outages due to equipment failure or maintenance increase this unbalance. Of most concern is the effect of unbalanced voltages on three-phase rotating electrical machines which is examined by the author. The loads however draw fluctuating currents with the highest levels only occurring for relatively infrequent short periods and this needs to be considered in arriving at an economic solution to the problem. It is shown that the predominant effects are rotor and stator heating and that the performance limits are a function of time of application as well as absolute level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Signalling system for German high speed lines
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: A few years ago, a renaissance of railways started all over Europe to increase the market share in long distance travel. The increase in passenger volume of the French TGV-lines confirmed the assumption, that higher travel speeds would attract more passengers. In Germany, the target was set to be half as fast as the plane, twice as fast as the car. The author shows how, to meet this target, new lines, new rolling stock and an upgraded signalling system had to be built. In addition, it was decided to upgrade existing lines in order to increase speed above 200 km/h.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of the three-phase drive technique in electric motive power units of the German Federal Railway
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Costs, serviceability, availability and low energy consumption, altogether the efficiency of the use of motive power units, are of major importance for the operating results of every company. Therefore, it has always been the objective of the German Federal Railway to increase the economic results of traction, wherever possible. In this connection, the author attaches particular importance to electric motive power units.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An electronic freight locomotive
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Class 10El is a 3000 kW, 126 tonne, 6 axle locomotive for operation on any part of the South African Railways 3 kV DC, 1065 mm gauge system. The authors describe the performance mechanical parts, traction motors, microprocessor control system, auxiliary circuits, and equipment layout.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Controllers for traction inverter drives
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors present a study of two different types of controllers for a traction voltage source inverter (VSI) drive. The first is a simple scalar control scheme which ensures constant torque operation down to low motor speed. With this controller the inverter V/f characteristic is automatically varied to compensate for different levels of motor load. This type of controller is essentially designed for good steady state operation over a wide range of inverter frequency. The second controller is based on state feedback control of the induction motor and is designed specifically to achieve a good transient response requirement. The author shoes that with this type of controller it is possible to achieve near decoupled flux and torque control as is possible with DC traction drives. The transient and steady state results obtained with this controller are described in detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations for semiconductor packaging (effects of semiconductor package reliability and life expectancy)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors deal with computer-aided system simulation to predict switching and conduction losses to evaluate electrical and thermal stresses on the semiconductors (GTOs) used in PWM inverters. They deal with the semiconductor packages developed primarily for cyclic applications and presents a comparison of the transient thermal impedance of various packaging concepts. In addition, they elaborate upon an easy, serviceable packaging concept, which also eliminates air flow through the enclosure, providing a contamination-free system. These packaging concepts were developed for, and are now used on, Seattle AC drive trolley coaches.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: VVVF inverter equipment for EMUs
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Introduction of AC induction motor drives into suburban high speed EMUs is carried out extensively in Japan. The authors describe the high power GTO (GTO thyristor) voltage source inverter which drives eight motors. The 3000 A 4500 V GTO and the heat-pipes are very useful for the reduction in size and weight of the equipment, and the new gate drive circuit has also helped to this purpose.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low loss GTO thyristors for rail traction applications
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: One of the most important characteristics of a GTO thyristor designed for rail traction applications is that of low energy losses. The authors presents the design features of high power GTO thyristors which achieve a reduction in both the on-state and switching losses.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The design and development of the Class 91 locomotive
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The British Rail Class 91 locomotive is a 25 kV Bo-Bo locomotive with a rated power of 4.54 MW and a design speed of 225 km/h. The locomotive will haul up to 11 Mk IV coaches and a driving trailer on the newly electrified East Coast Main Line from London to Edinburgh. In addition sleeper trains of up to 750 tonnes will be hauled on the West Coast Main Line including the arduous ascents of Shap and Beattock. The contract was placed by British Rail in February 1986. The authors describe the design and development of the power circuit, microprocessor control system and mechanical parts. Particular emphasis is given to the novel aspects of the design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The design, construction and operation of the overheat fixed equipment for the Queensland Railways main line electrification project
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Over the last ten years Queensland Railways have experienced a massive expansion in the amount of overhead equipment installed and by mid 1989 will have approximately 2467 single track kilometres of 25 kV overhead catenary. It is important the QR should now concentrate on the most economical way of maintaining the catenary system. One such method which should reduce maintenance costs is a Track and Overhead Inspection and Recording car which is due for delivery later this year. Experience to date has shown that the catenary system installed should accommodate the traffic requirement of Queensland Railways for many years to come with a minimum of maintenance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vacuum circuit breakers for AC traction vehicles
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: GEC Traction has been involved with the design and manufacture of vehicle mounted vacuum circuit breakers (VCBs) for nearly twenty years. Situated on the roof near to the pantograph, this primary circuit breaker provides the locomotive or multiple-unit with protection against fault currents. It also isolates the vehicle whilst passing through earthed section gaps in the overhead catenary wire. This latter function accounts for the great majority of switching operations, there being, typically, on section gap every twenty kilometres on an inter-city 25 kV system. The author describes aspects of the latest VCB design, together with details of performance tests and the developments of a suitable high-strength polymeric insulator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New generation signalling control centre
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Easter weekend 1989 saw the commissioning of British Rail's first Integrated Electronic Control Centre (IECC). This event marked a major change in signalling technology where mimic diagrams were replaced by colour monitors and train routesetting and regulation is now an automatic function with manual intervention if required. Liverpool Street was the first of the new generation signalling control centres to be brought into service and was closely followed by the first stage of the new control centre at York.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A strategic approach to railway signalling software
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Recent developments in microelectronic technology have revealed that they offer a technically superior performance to railway signalling at a lower cost, and microelectronics is now being applied to almost every vital signalling function. In order to achieve a high level of reliability and safety in the software it is essential that tight managerial controls are adopted throughout all stages of development, manufacture, operation and maintenance. Safety requirements, specifications, system design and software design should be well defined and documented. These approaches to software for railway signalling are all compiled in a set of guidelines. They have been built on the long experience in the relay-based signalling and deliberate investigation on the application of microelectronics to signalling, and they are being improved through new experience in the microelectronic signalling age. The authors describe these activities in developing and evaluating the software for railway signalling in Japan.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Overhead equipment for BR main line electrification
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author looks at the development of BR overhead equipment for 25 kV AC electrification since its inception in 1956. The author describes the Mark IIIB overhead equipment used for electrification. The changes and improvements in design and installation methods which have taken place since 1972, with particular reference to the East Coast Main Line electrification, are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: 25kV AC single phase circuit breakers-30 years of development
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author outlines the development and application of 25kV, single phase, AC circuit breakers to British Rail (BR) electrification schemes over the past thirty years. The use of bulk oil breakers on the early main line electrification between Euston, Manchester and Liverpool and other lines and the minimum oil circuit breakers on the original 25kV portion of the Great Eastern line electrification is examined. The issues involved in the decision to move from oil circuit breakers to vacuum circuit breakers for the extension of the West Coast electrification from Weaver Junction to Glasgow in the mid 1970's are reviewed. The author also examines recent changes in the design and enclosure of 25kV switchgear and discusses the application of such equipment to future British Rail electrification projects from an operational, maintenance and economic viewpoint.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Relay interlockings do have a future
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The author shows that relay interlockings can be produced and used cost effectively. Of all the interlocking techniques available in South Africa, the optimized, geographic relay interlocking is still the cheapest. The principle of open tender amongst the railway signalling contractors will always apply for the supply of interlockings and, until the prices and cost of maintenance of other types of interlocking prove their cost effectiveness, relay based interlockings will be utilized.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Operation simulator of heavy haul train
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: A train operation simulator is developed. It can be applied to train dynamics research, driver training and railway management especially those of heavy haul train with electric locomotives. The simulator is composed of a main computer system, graphic display system and training environment. A model of train dynamic action, which takes vibrations of every car in six degrees of freedom (longitudinal, lateral, vertical, roll, pitch and yaw motion) into consideration, is established and realized on computer. Operation results are output on the printer, plotter and graphic terminal. Although only a microcomputer is used as a main computer, this simulator can simulate a train with up to 200 cars in real time.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Tangara train management system-concept, design and experience
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: Tangara, an aboriginal word meaning 'to go', is the name chosen for Sydney's new mainline double deck commuter train. During the conceptual design stage it was realised that to reduce operational delays caused by train faults and decrease maintenance/repair time an intelligent means of fault handling and recording was required. This need gave rise to the Tangara train management system (TMS) which although being similar in concept to other systems being installed on modern locomotives and rolling-stock, is unique and specific in design to Tangara. Three basic functions are performed by the train management system: equipment monitoring; fault annunciation; and remote control. Each function, in turn, is examined by the authors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cost-benefit analysis of the electrification of the Beira Alta Line in Portugal
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The Beira Alta Line is part of the main network of the Portuguese State Railway, and links Pampilhosa (on the line Lisbon-Porto) with the Spanish frontier. It was seen as inevitable that a basic renewal of this line would have to be undertaken, and to this end, the authors detail how a cost-benefit analysis for the electrification of the Beira Alta Line was carried out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation model of AC/DC traction converters and drives for the calculation of input power characteristics
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: The authors present a model for the simulation of AC/DC thyristor controlled traction vehicles. A FORTRAN program for the simulation of such a vehicle is developed. It is based on a modern numerical methods library and runs on a mainframe computer. Efficiency of Runge-Kutte Adams and Gears integration methods are compared. The Adams variable stage, variable order predictor corrector method proves to be the most efficient, although Gears method is shown to be insensitive to the circuit stiffness. A simple closed loop control circuit is applied to reach a desired steady state as quickly as possible and a new quasi steady state is reached usually in less than ten line voltage periods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Methods of improving the voltage regulation on 25 kV electric railways
publicationTitle: International Conference on Main Line Railway Electrification 1989
abstract: In Australia, commercial and operating pressures are dictating the running of fewer but larger trains for a specified traffic task. The railway power supply design (and therefore the infrastructure costs) are however governed by the instantaneous power demands of the train and the spacing between trains. It is far easier to optimise infrastructure costs and achieve a high load factor on a railway power system which supplies, European style, many trains each of relatively small magnitude, than to supply a smaller number of large trains. The problems are further aggravated in Australia by the weak, radially-fed power systems and the random nature of freight train operations. The author documents a range of options which can be used, selectively, to optimise the power system design on a new electrification project, or to enhance an existing AC electrification at any voltage or frequency. On a new electrification project, these techniques have the potential to reduce the power supply infrastructure costs by about 10% compared with compared with conventional systems based on normal European practices.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
